editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech contains one concrete offer, and it qualifies our earlier reading that Andy Burnham's pitch to Holyrood was aimed only at Edinburgh's powers. Employment support run by the Department for Work and Pensions is reserved to Westminster. Offering Scotland a localised model 'shaped by Holyrood' would mean London giving something up, not just asking Edinburgh to.

The offer comes with conditions. It must go 'right down' and follow the 'Easterhouse principle', so Holyrood would receive the power only on the understanding that it passes it on to regions. That is devolution with a design brief attached, and it puts the First Minister in an awkward spot. Refusing means turning down powers. Accepting means conceding the Prime Minister's claim that Scotland is over-centralised.

The cooperation he holds up as the model is small. It is £10 million from each government for two defence colleges, set against a defence sector he says supports 12,000 Scottish jobs. Even the forum is new: the National Economic Council meeting with the first ministers will be its first since he took office in July.

Burnham traces Scotland's regional weakness to decisions taken 'hundreds of miles away', with Ravenscraig as his example. Part of what he now calls missing once existed. Strathclyde and Scotland's other regional councils were abolished in 1996, a Westminster reorganisation the speech does not mention. His City Region Deals and 'new model of regional empowerment' are partly an attempt to rebuild a tier of government the UK state removed.

His procurement promise also carries a cost the speech only half admits. Choosing Falkirk-built buses meant paying 'a little more'. Applied across all UK public procurement, that is a standing subsidy to domestic manufacturing, and its price has not been put to Parliament or to the Treasury.
